### XV. TANSIL.

Here you see a snake <note>original: "serpe"</note> that languishes in the snow where a digger had thrown it; and a naked child <note>original: "fanciullo"</note> burning in the midst of the fire, with certain other minute details, with the motto that says, IDEM, ITIDEM, NON IDEM. This seems to me to be an enigma rather than anything else, so I do not trust myself to explain it completely. Yet I would believe that it wishes to signify the same troublesome fate, which torments one and the other in the same way, that is, most intensely, without mercy, unto death, with different instruments or contrary principles, showing itself to be the same in cold and heat. Since religion resides in the highest things in man, and from the highest things his lower things live and shine, and because Mahomet is present in their minds together with their religion, therefore some Mahomet is always placed in their view. And so that they may turn their faces toward the East, over which the Lord is, he is placed below the Christian center. It is not the Mahomet himself who wrote the <term>Alcoranum</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss>, but another who performs his office, nor is it always the same one, but he is changed. Once it was a man from Saxony who, having been captured by the Algerians, became a Mahometan; because he had also been a Christian, he was sometimes led to speak with them about the Lord, that He was not the son of Joseph, but the Son of God Himself. To this Mahomet, others succeeded later. In the place where that representative Mahomet has his seat, a fire appears like a torch, so that he may be recognized; but that fire is not visible to anyone other than Mahometans.

830. The Mahomet himself who wrote the <term>Alcoranum</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss> does not come into view today. It has been told to me that in the earliest times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all things of their religion as God, he was ejected from his seat, which he had held under the Catholics, and was lowered to the right side near the south. Once a certain society of Mahometans was incited by malicious spirits to acknowledge Mahomet as God. So that the sedition might be quieted, Mahomet was taken from the lower earth and shown, and at that time he was also seen by me. He appeared similar to bodily spirits, to whom there is no interior perception, with his face tending toward black, and I heard him speaking these words, *I am your Mahomet*; and he soon seemed as if sinking.

831. Mahometans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the faith of the three Divine Persons and, from that, the worship of three Gods and as many Creators. Furthermore, they are hostile to the Roman Catholics because of their genuflections before images, and because of this they call the latter idolaters and the former fanatics, saying that they make a three-headed God, and that they say "one" but mutter "three," and consequently that they cut up Omnipotence and make three out of one and of the one. And that thus they are like fauns with three horns, one for each god, and together three for one, and that thus they pray, thus they sing, and thus they sound from the pulpits.

832. Mahometans, like all nations that acknowledge one God and love what is just and do good from religion, have their own Heaven, but it is outside the Christian one. However, the Mahometan Heaven is divided into two. In the lower one, they live honestly with several wives, but from there no others are raised into the higher Heaven except those who renounce concubines and acknowledge our Lord the Savior, and at the same time His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I have heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of God the Father. This faith is among them, through which ascent into the higher Heaven is given to them by the Lord.

833. The fact that the Mahometan religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian religion can be a scandal to those who think about Divine Providence and at the same time believe that no one can be saved except one who was born a Christian. But the Mahometan religion is not a scandal to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these inquire in what it consists, and they also find it. It is in this: that the Mahometan religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the Wisest of all, and also as the Son of God. But because they have made only the <term>Alcoranum</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss> the book of their religion, and hence Mahomet, who wrote it, has settled into their thoughts, and they follow him with some worship, they therefore think little about our Lord. It often happened <note>clarification: to him</note> that the sharpness of his eloquence escaped him. In his manner of living he was not simple, but even in the height of moderation <note>original: "σωφροσύνῃ"</note> he practiced a certain luxury. He was accustomed to indulge in white clothing and to bathe twice every day in the public baths. And when someone once asked him why, being a bishop, he bathed twice a day, he replied: Because I cannot manage a third time. On one occasion, while he was seeing the bishop Sergius, he was asked by one of those around Arsakius why he wore clothing unsuited to a bishop, and where it was written that a consecrated man should dress in white. He said, You tell me first where it is written that the bishop should wear black clothing. When the questioner was at a loss, Sisinnius followed up his counter-question: Indeed, you would not be able to show that the consecrated man must be dressed in black. But Solomon advised me, saying: Let your garments be white <note>context: Ecclesiastes 9:8</note>. And the Savior in the Gospels appears using white clothing. Furthermore, he showed Moses and Elijah wearing white to the apostles. Having said these and many other things readily, he was greatly admired by those present. When Leontius, the bishop of Ancyra in Galatia Minor, was taking away a church of the Novatians <term>Navatianoí</term> <gloss>followers of Novatian</gloss> while visiting Constantinople, Sisinnius went to him and appealed for him to restore the church. He <note>clarification: Leontius</note> met him warmly and said to him: You Novatians ought not to have churches, you who abolish repentance <term>metanoia</term> <gloss>penitence/change of mind</gloss> and shut out the loving-kindness of God. When Leontius said these and many other such things disparagingly to the Novatians, Sisinnius said: And yet no one has repented <term>metanóēsen</term> as I have. When the other asked again, How have you repented? Sisinnius answered: Because I have seen you. When John the bishop <note>context: John Chrysostom</note> once brought a charge against him and said that the city could not have two bishops, Sisinnius said: For it does not have <note>clarification: two</note>. When John became angry and said, You see that you alone are a bishop by decree <note>alternative: or "by your own counsel"</note>, Sisinnius said: I do not mean that, but that I am not a bishop in your eyes alone, as I am to those who hear <note>clarification: my teaching</note>. John, being annoyed at what was said, said: I shall stop you from speaking, for you are a heretic. To this Sisinnius replied gracefully: Indeed, I would even pay a reward if you would release me from such great labor. John, being softened by the reply, said: I would not stop you from your freedom of speech <term>parrhēsia</term> <gloss>boldness/frankness</gloss> if speaking at all distresses you. Thus was Sisinnius ready in his replies and graceful. To write down these things and record what was said by him would be a long task. For this reason, I have shown in a few words what kind of man he was, having considered it necessary to lead with this. And I say this, that all know him for his education; and because of this, all the bishops in succession loved and honored him. Moreover, all the prominent men of the Senate cherished and admired him. Many books have been written by him, but in them he uses a particular style and mixes in poetic expressions. He was more admired when speaking than when being read. For such grace was in him, in his face and his voice, and in his posture, and in his look, and in the whole movement of his body. He was loved for these things by all religions, and especially by the bishop Atticus. And so much for the matters concerning Sisinnius.

Suppose now that a person wishes, by means of a life annuity, to assure to his heirs a capital payable at the end of the year of his death. To determine the value of this annuity, one can imagine that the person borrows as a life annuity this capital divided by unity increased by the rate of interest, and that he invests it at perpetual interest at the same office. It is clear that this capital will be owed by the office to his heirs at the end of the year of his death; but he will have paid, each year, only the excess of the life interest over the perpetual interest. The table of life annuities therefore makes known what the person must pay annually to the office to assure this capital after his death.

Maritime insurance, insurance against fire and storms, and generally all establishments of this kind, are calculated by the same principles. A merchant has ships at sea; he wishes to insure their value and that of their cargo against the dangers they may run. For this, he gives a sum to a company, which guarantees to him the estimated value of his cargoes and his ships. The ratio of this value to the sum that must be given as the price of the insurance depends on the dangers to which the ships are exposed, and can only be assessed by numerous observations on the fate of ships having departed from the port for the same destination.

"And He rode upon a Cherub" <note>clarification: singular</note> is when the King is not settled upon His throne. "He who sits upon the Cherubim" <note>clarification: plural</note> is two. Woe to the world when one Cherub turns his face away from his companion, for behold it is written:
> with their faces toward one another <note>Exodus 25:20</note>

When there was peace in the world. **Rabbi Isaac** said: we have learned, "Do not uncover the nakedness of a daughter-in-law or a daughter," woe to him who uncovers their nakedness in this manner. It is written concerning Jacob, "passing through from end to end." And thus the portion of Israel with the Holy One, blessed be He, is found in their ornaments, in the manner of that which is above, as it is written:
> Israel, in whom I will be glorified <note>Isaiah 49:3</note>

Come and see, **Rabbi Isaac** <note>clarification: said</note>: in former days, when one said to his companion, "Show me one vessel and take money for it." > And your people are all righteous, they shall inherit the land forever; the branch of my planting, the work of my hands, that I may be glorified <note>Isaiah 60:21</note>

Woe that it should be filled and that money should be sustained. **Rabbi Isaac** said: Woe, for I see those who are circumcised, all those who are crowned from the higher knots, they have searched. Woe that it should be filled, for all of them are suspended below, woe. A window opened among us, it opened and they are sharpened and prepared from the smoke for the order that rests upon them. And as in the Book of Concealment <term>Sifra de-Tzniuta</term> <gloss>The Book of Modesty/Secrets</gloss> it is proven: woe above, woe below, and all of them rise in one balance. Who is the dread of the Book? **Rabbi Hezekiah said**: these sections are all in the Great Palace <term>Heikhal</term> <gloss>Palace/Temple</gloss> and they fill the whole earth. **Rabbi Yehuda** <note>clarification: said</note>: all of them are thus, and from this they are superior. **Rabbi said**: Woe to him who inclines and bends, and to him who does not go up and bend to them thus.

### The Parable of the Wheat

A parable of a man who lived among the fields and did not know the dwellers of the city. He sowed wheat and ate the wheat in its raw form. One day he entered the city; they brought before him a good loaf of bread. He said: what is this for? They said: it is bread to eat. He ate and it tasted very sweet. **The Rabbi said**: from what is this made? They said: wheat. Later they brought before him cakes kneaded in oil. He tasted them and said: what are these made of? They said: wheat. Later they brought before him the royal pastries <term>tariki</term> <gloss>fine honey-cakes</gloss> made with honey and oil. He said: and these sweets, from what were they made? They said: wheat. He said: surely I am the master of all these things, for I eat the essence of all these, which is wheat. And because of that...

<margin>Su's Commentary <note>context: Su Che (1039–1112), a Song dynasty statesman and scholar.</note></margin>Those who do not know the Way <term>Dao</term> but devote themselves to learning find that what they hear and see increases daily, yet they have nothing with which to unify it; this inevitably becomes a burden. Confucius said: "Hear much, select what is good and follow it; see much and remember it; this is the second level of knowledge." If one day you know the Way, you will look upon the false as false; nothing is not a delusion. Removing delusion to return to nature is what is meant by "decrease." Confucius said to Zigong: "Do you think I am one who learns much and remembers it all?" He replied: "Yes, is it not so?" Confucius said: "No, I unify it all with one principle." Forgetting the mind to purely return to nature is what is called "decrease." If delusions still remain, then one must simultaneously forget this mind to purely return to nature until nothing remains; only then does one depart from "doing" <term>wei</term> without failing at "non-doing" <term>wu wei</term>. All people have desires and a mind that wishes to take the world and finish its affairs; thus they create tasks and seek after them. Their mind is visible externally, and things <note>clarification: external objects or people</note> dislike it; therefore they meet with difficulty and cannot succeed. The Sage practices non-doing, thus his mind is without affairs. When his mind is visible externally, things are at peace with it. Although he does not take the world's affairs to act upon them, the world's affairs follow and find peace therein.

<margin>Lu's Commentary <note>context: Lu Huiqing (1035–1111), a Song dynasty official known for his commentaries on the classics.</note></margin>To practice learning <note>original: "為學" (wei xue)</note> is the state of one who has not yet heard the Way. One who has not heard the Way and seeks it cannot avoid being broad; therefore it is said to "increase." To practice the Way <note>original: "為道" (wei dao)</note> is the state of one who has already heard the Way. Having heard the Way and practicing it, one can only practice non-doing; therefore it is said to "decrease." "Decreasing and further decreasing" refers to those who have not yet avoided "doing." When even the act of decreasing is decreased, one then reaches non-doing. Non-doing means being still and unmoving. "Doing nothing left undone" means being stimulated and thus penetrating the causes of all under heaven. To reach non-doing through non-doing is called the constant. Learning without worry is called divine. The Way of the divine is called the Way. Who but the most divine can participate in this? Viewed from this perspective, taking the world is always done through non-doing; as for those who use "doing," it is clear they are insufficient to take the world.

A divine water-jar <note>original: "Θεία δ’ ὑδρεία"</note>, or one gushing water over heaven and earth, they represent by likening the water-jar to a heart that has a tongue. It is likened to a heart because among them this is the ruling part of the body, just as the Nile stands as the ruler of Egypt. It is likened to a tongue because this <note>clarification: the tongue</note> always exists in moisture, and they call it the generator of that which is good. There are two water-jars, neither more nor less, because the work of the rising <note>clarification: of the river</note> according to them is two-fold. They place one under the land of Egypt, since Egypt is by itself a generator of water. They place the other under the Ocean; for water also arrives from it into Egypt at the time of the rising. They place corn <note>clarification: grain</note> under the rains which occur in the southern parts of Ethiopia at the time of the rising of the Nile. That Egypt generates the water is possible to learn from this: for in the rest of the climate of the world, the floods of the rivers are completed in the winter.
